result.summary: Orpheus sings of Myrrha, who conceives an incestuous passion for her father Cinyras and tries to hang herself, but her nurse stops her and arranges a night with Cinyras in the dark. When Cinyras discovers the truth he chases her with a sword; pregnant, she flees, prays to be changed, and becomes the myrrh tree, from which Adonis is born.

scenes.title: Poet's warning about Myrrha
scenes.summary: The narrator warns daughters and parents away from this horrible tale and says the fault was not Cupid's but a Fury's. He rejoices that such crimes are far from his own land.

scenes.title: Myrrha struggles with her desire
scenes.summary: Myrrha argues with herself about her forbidden passion. When Cinyras asks what husband she wants, she answers 'One like thyself'.
scenes.stakes: Her honour and her father's trust, if her desire is revealed or acted on.

scenes.title: The nurse prevents her suicide
scenes.summary: At midnight Myrrha tries to hang herself. The nurse saves her, learns the secret, and promises help.
scenes.stakes: Myrrha's life, since she will die unless she can have her father.

scenes.title: The night in the dark
scenes.summary: During the festival of Ceres, when Cenchreïs is away, the nurse brings Myrrha to the drunken Cinyras. After several nights he lights a lamp and discovers his daughter.
scenes.stakes: Myrrha risks exposure and horror at committing the crime; Cinyras is unknowingly defiled.

scenes.title: Flight and transformation
scenes.summary: Cinyras draws his sword and Myrrha flees to Sabæa. There she prays to be neither living nor dead and turns into a myrrh tree.
scenes.stakes: Her life from her father's sword, and the fate of her unborn child.

scenes.title: Birth of Adonis
scenes.summary: Lucina helps the tree to open and the child is born. The Naiads anoint him with myrrh tears.
scenes.stakes: The life of the newborn child.

alias_notes.explanation: The summary spells the queen's name Cenchris; the verse uses Cenchreïs.

notable_quotes.reason: Myrrha's prayer to be denied both life and death, prompting her transformation.
The narrator's unusual warning to daughters and parents before the tale.
Myrrha's rationalization that human laws forbid what nature permits.

analysis.text: The tale shows forbidden passion as a punishment inflicted by the gods, and ends in a transformation that is both penalty and mercy. It continues Orpheus' song of unlawful loves.
Myrrha's appeals to animal behaviour and to foreign customs reflect Roman debate about nature versus law. The setting in Arabia and Cyprus ties myrrh to the exotic East.

legacy.text: The Myrrha story influenced later literature, including Alfieri's tragedy Mirra (1789) and Dante's mention of Mirra in the Inferno.

fun_facts.text: Myrrh is a real aromatic resin from Commiphora trees of Arabia and the Horn of Africa, and Ovid's tale gives it a mythic origin.

language_notes.text: 'Without issue' means without children; Cinyras would have been counted happy had he never had a child, since Myrrha is the source of his ruin.
Ismarian refers to Ismarus, a mountain in Thrace. Ovid means Thracian women, and so his own region, as free of such a crime; the speaker here is Orpheus.
Panchæan land is Panchaia, a legendary island in the east, famed for spices and incense. Amomum and zedoary are aromatic plants.
The three Sisters are the Furies (Eumenides), goddesses of vengeance. Stygian means of the river Styx, the underworld.
The braces mark words the translator supplies; the narrator is reporting Myrrha's inner struggle, and the translation is in the old style with thou/thee forms.
Myrrha cites animal mating as precedent for incest, an argument from 'nature' versus human law.
Nations said to permit incest: a vague reference to foreign peoples, probably Eastern customs known by report; the translator's footnote 44 glosses it.
'Fatal delusion' means her self-deceiving hope that staying near him is harmless.
The Sisters with snakes for hair are the Furies (Eumenides), avenging goddesses who torment the guilty with torches and serpents.
'Inquires of herself' means he asks her directly, while listing the suitors' names.
The tree simile is rendered in a long, looping sentence; "is dreaded in each direction" means bystanders fear it may fall on them whichever way it tips.
"Girdle" means a belt or sash worn around the waist; here it serves as the rope for her noose.
"Halter" is a noose or hanging rope.
"In this slow manner" means she regrets that her suicide attempt was slow and so allowed discovery; the sense is compressed and slightly obscure.
"Charms" are magical spells or incantations; the nurse lists folk remedies of magic, herbs and sacrifice.
"Presentiment" means a feeling that something is so, before it is known; the nurse suspects ordinary love.
"Happy in thy husband" is a veiled hint: Myrrha envies her mother for having Cinyras as husband, revealing the forbidden object of her love.
The broken-off sentence ("thy----") shows the nurse recoiling from naming the father; she nonetheless swears to help.
The festival is the Thesmophoria-like rite of Ceres (the Greek Demeter), when married women observed ritual chastity, which is why Cenchreïs is away from the marriage bed.
Boötes (the Wagoner) and the Triones (the seven stars of the Plough or Great Bear) mark the constellations' turning, meaning deep night, past midnight.
Icarus and his daughter Erigone were placed in the heavens as stars (Boötes and Virgo); the stars hide so as not to witness a daughter's crime against her father.
"Hams" here means the backs of the knees.
"Doomed" translates a word of ill omen: the union is fated and accursed, not merely forbidden.
"His own bowels" means his own offspring, flesh of his flesh, a harsh way to stress the incest.
The Arabians and the Panchæan fields refer to Arabia, a land famous for palms and spices; Panchaia was a legendary incense-producing island or region in the east.
"Nine horns of the moon" means nine lunar months, the length of her pregnancy; the moon's crescent is imagined as horns.
Sabæan: of Saba (Sheba) in southern Arabia, a land known in antiquity for frankincense and myrrh.
She asks to be neither among the living nor the dead, so that she pollutes neither realm; hence she begs for transformation.
Distil means to fall in drops; here the myrrh resin oozes from the bark like tears.
Lucina is the goddess of childbirth, invoked by women in labour; the tree-mother cannot call on her, having lost her voice.
"Even Envy herself" means that even someone inclined to find fault would praise the child's beauty.

context_notes.text: The narrator is Orpheus, who sings these tales after losing Eurydice. Myrrha's story is one of his songs about forbidden loves.
Cupid (Love) shoots arrows and carries torches that inspire desire. Here he is cleared; the passion is attributed to a Fury's infernal fire.
Cinyras is king of Cyprus and Myrrha's father; in this myth she later conceives Adonis by him.
Her mother, Cenchreis, would become her rival; Myrrha lists the tangled family names incest would create.
Cinyras is king of Cyprus and Myrrha's father; her love for him is the incestuous passion at the center of this fable.
A nurse in ancient households was often a lifelong confidante, close to her charge like a second mother, which explains her devotion here.
Appealing to the cradle and nursing was a powerful plea, invoking the nurse's maternal claim over the girl.
Cinyras is king of Cyprus; the nurse exploits his drunkenness and the queen's absence, deceiving him about the girl's identity.
Cinyras, Myrrha's father, has just discovered that she tricked him into incest in the dark; he now tries to kill her.
Myrrh is an aromatic resin from trees of the genus Commiphora, prized for perfume and incense; the myth explains its origin.
Naiads are freshwater nymphs. The child is Adonis, later beloved of Venus.

literary_notes.text: The poet addresses daughters and parents directly, warning them off. It heightens the horror and shows his moral discomfort.
The long list of Panchaia's precious spices is offered as a poor trade, implying no wealth could justify the myrrh-tree's origin.
Cupid is made to speak and defend himself, shifting blame from love to a Fury and her serpents.
The poet bitterly urges Myrrha to choose among countless suitors, stressing the one man she must not choose.
Myrrha addresses the gods and abstract natural affection directly, dramatizing her desperate plea against her own desire.
'So much mine, he is not mine' turns the family bond into the very barrier, expressing her torment.
A string of questions makes Myrrha accuse herself, piling up the confused family relationships her act would create.
Myrrha's reply, 'One like thyself,' carries a hidden meaning that the reader grasps and Cinyras does not.
Cinyras praises her answer and urges her to stay affectionate, unknowingly encouraging the very love that will destroy them.
Her passion is called an "unconquerable flame," picturing love as a consuming fire.
Myrrha's wavering mind is compared to a tree about to fall, conveying how close she is to collapse and the danger around her.
Myrrha's furious flight and shame show she knows her desire is wrong, making her more tragic than simply wicked.
The nurse's hair bristling and bones chilling dramatize her horror at the realization.
The nurse breaks off mid-sentence, leaving the unspeakable word unsaid and so stressing the horror of the taboo.
Moon, clouds and stars withdraw as if unwilling to witness the deed, making nature mirror the moral darkness.
The stumbling foot and the funereal owl are ill omens that signal the disaster to come.
Repeated "now" quickens the pace, tracing each step toward the room and intensifying Myrrha's mounting dread.
The narrator notes that the words "father" and daughter-like endearments fit the scene, bitterly making the proper family names part of the horror.
Light finally brings discovery, reversing the darkness that hid the truth; the lamp's revelation marks the story's turning point.
Night is given a favouring will, as if the darkness itself rescues Myrrha from death.
The step-by-step conversion of bones, blood, arms and fingers into wood, sap and branches shows the body becoming a tree, in Ovid's typical metamorphosis style.
The tale explains the origin of myrrh and its name, turning her tears into a lasting product.
The groaning, weeping tree makes the mother's suffering visible even though she cannot speak, evoking sympathy.
The baby's beauty is compared to painted Cupids, introducing Adonis as a figure of erotic charm.
